input.question: Why do we have to consciencley swallow a liquid, what is inhibiting it from merely sliding down our throats?
input.ground_truth: Because normally, our airways are open unconsciously, with the epiglottis standing strait up, allowing air to flow in and out. When we swollow, the muscles in our throat push on the epiglottis, closing the larynx, guiding the food to the esophagus and stomach. So, if we were to allow saliva or other fluids to just slide down, without swallowing, it wouldn't be guided into the stomach, it would be guided down our bronchi and lungs, since the airway wouldn't close. messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why do we have to consciencley swallow a liquid, what is inhibiting it from merely sliding down our throats?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have a little cup of juice. When you tip the cup and let the juice come out, what happens? The juice just falls out, right? But your mouth and throat aren't like a cup. When you want to swallow juice, your body has to help the juice go down the right way, so it doesn't go into your nose or get you coughing.

So, when you swallow on purpose (that's what "consciously" means—doing it on purpose), you use your tongue and some muscles to help push the juice down. If you just let the juice sit in your mouth and don't help it go down, it might just sit there or dribble out of the corner of your mouth, or even go up your nose by accident! That's why your body has to work a little to make sure the juice goes down your throat and into your tummy the right way. 

The things that help this happen are called muscles, and they work like little helpers to move the juice along. That's what's "inhibiting" (or helping to control) the juice from just sliding down by itself—it needs a little help from your body!
